projects.title: Pet Shelter
projects.content: A trivia game with a pet shelter metagame: rescue runaway pets, care for them and rebuild their shelter. I was the team’s technical lead and second in charge, from first concepts to launch.

detail.summary: A new trivia game for etermax with a pet shelter metagame: answer the neighbors’ questions to find runaway pets, care for them and rebuild the shelter. I was technical lead and second in charge, from first concepts to launch. The trivia version missed its targets, and etermax later relaunched it as a merge game.
detail.client: Pet Shelter by Trivia Crack is a mobile trivia game from etermax, the Buenos Aires studio behind Trivia Crack.
detail.context: The shelter went through hard times and its pets ran away. That premise had to become a whole visual world around the trivia: a town to explore, neighbors who give clues, pets to rescue and care for, and a shelter that grows as you play. I started with the concepts, then worked with the team to take the art to launch.
detail.role: Principal Product Artist: technical lead and second in charge of the team. Concept art and illustration, UI/UX design and Unity integration.

projects.title: Nearpod
projects.content: I designed image answers for quizzes and a Motion UI menu for the iPad app of an award-winning US edtech platform.

detail.summary: Two projects for Nearpod’s lesson platform: images in quiz answers and a Motion UI menu that brought new lesson libraries to the iPad app.
detail.client: Nearpod is an award-winning student engagement platform that teachers use to run interactive lessons. As a senior product designer at Hexacta, I worked with Nearpod’s US-based product team on new features for its web and iPad apps.
detail.context: The web app was evolving fast, the iPad app had to keep up, and new features had to work on both. I often stepped in as a firefighter, solving design problems the team was stuck on.
detail.role: Product designer (and firefighter): prototyping, UI design, heuristics and accessibility.

sections.heading: Case study: Image Quiz
sections.text:
Nearpod had just redesigned its quiz activity when the product owner asked for a new feature: images in the answers.

The quiz has two sides. On the teacher side, a small improvement to the existing view was enough. The student side needed more: it had to become engaging for kids.

sections.caption: Teacher side, before: the freshly redesigned quiz editor.
sections.alt: Nearpod quiz editor for teachers, before images were added

sections.caption: Student side, before: it worked, but it was kind of boring.
sections.alt: Nearpod student quiz with plain text answers

sections.heading: Teacher side
sections.text: The editor component was already built in React, so I kept the change small: an image button next to each answer field.
sections.caption: A small tweak: an image button next to each answer.
sections.alt: Quiz editor with an image button beside each answer option

sections.caption: Once an image is added, the answer text becomes optional.
sections.alt: Quiz editor with a photo added to an answer, text marked optional

sections.heading: Student side
sections.text: For kids, I turned the answers into a colorful, game-board-like grid of image cards.
sections.caption: Colors and a game-board feel bring the student side to life.
sections.alt: Student quiz with six colorful image answer cards

sections.caption: A magnifier lets students take a closer look at any image.
sections.alt: Student quiz with a magnifier icon on an image card

sections.caption: Images open in Nearpod’s standard lightbox.
sections.alt: An answer image enlarged in a lightbox

sections.caption: Big, clear selection states and a Submit button sized for kids.
sections.alt: Two image answers selected and an active Submit button

sections.heading: Case study: Motion UI
sections.text:
Nearpod sold free and paid lessons in a store, then added custom libraries for schools, districts and programs. These had to be available on every platform.

On the web, a top navigation bar with drop-down menus handled it fine. On iOS, it was a different game, and the team had been struggling to find an answer before I joined.
notes: Nearpod wanted more revenue from premade lessons
The web app was evolving much faster than iOS

sections.heading: Welcome
sections.text:
This was the iPad Welcome screen. Stakeholders saw it almost as part of the brand and didn’t want it changed.

So instead of redesigning it, I proposed Motion UI: a smooth transition from the Welcome menu into a new submenu, like the Flash sites of the old days.

The heads of Product and iOS loved the idea, and we aligned on the solution.

projects.title: .ar domain launch
projects.content: Opening Argentina’s .ar domain to the public: 35,000 new domains registered in two months.

detail.client: NIC Argentina is the government office that runs the .ar country-code top-level domain. I led the design work to open .ar domains to the public.
detail.context:
Until 2019, people could only register subdomains like .com.ar or .net.ar. Opening .ar itself was a big deal for the organization, and it had been delayed for years.

Four organizations shared the registration platform. Communication between them was poor, and our requests sat low on the platform provider’s list. So we focused on the teams we could work with and kept platform changes to a minimum, which meant the front end could only change in small ways.
detail.role: Lead designer: prototyping, UI design, heuristic evaluation, communications, branding and consulting.
notes: UI design had to use a government framework library
Platform redesign was out of scope

sections.caption: Where we started: domain search and the domain list.
sections.alt: NIC Argentina domain search and domain list

sections.heading: Opening phases
sections.text: To prevent speculation and domain squatting, the team designed a three-phase opening.
list: Phase 1: people who already owned a name as .com.ar or .net.ar got priority to register it as .ar. If two people had priority on the same name, a random drawing decided who got it.
Phase 2: anyone could request any name, and a random drawing picked among all requests.
Phase 3: open registration, like any other domain.
notes: This case study focuses on Phase 1
Case 1: one user with priority to register
Case 2: two users with priority to register

sections.heading: Tweak it
sections.text:
The process was complicated, and our resources were limited. So I asked: “What if, instead of changing everything, we tweak it a little?”

I focused on the domain list table. It was within our resources, and users already went there to renew their domains.

Right away I noticed the action buttons were icons only. I couldn’t tell what they did until I hovered over them: a real usability and accessibility problem, and a quick one to fix.
sections.caption: Before: icon-only actions in the domain list.
sections.alt: Domain list with icon-only action buttons

sections.caption: Renew, Transfer, Delegate: the labels only appeared on hover.
sections.alt: Renew, Transfer and Delegate icon buttons with hover labels

sections.text: First change: a new, highlighted row for the reserved domain, with a clear Register button.
sections.caption: Case 1: one person with priority gets a highlighted row and a Register button.
sections.alt: Domain list with a highlighted reserved row and a Register button

sections.text:
That solved Case 1. But what if two people have priority on the same domain?

That kicked off a UX writing debate that lasted days. Spanish has many near-synonyms with subtle differences, and the button label mattered. We landed on Registrar (Register) and Solicitar (Request).

Together with the Communications team, we also added an alert at the top of the page explaining the new rows and linking to details about the opening.
sections.caption: Case 2: Register and Request actions, plus an alert explaining the opening.
sections.alt: Domain list with Register and Request buttons and an information alert

sections.heading: Visual communication
sections.text:
There was no time for the big campaign we had planned, so we explained the opening with a landing page, emails and social media.

The concept: “Your place on the internet.” A new domain is a new world in cyberspace, so we went with a space theme.
sections.caption: The landing page: the new domain, its features, the opening timeline, and links to rules and FAQs.
sections.alt: Space-themed .ar landing page

sections.heading: Aftermath
sections.text:
Then the project stalled for almost a year because of the unstable platform, so we never got to test it with users.

A political decision brought it back to life, and the teams had to ship fast. The opening ran on a very tight schedule, and some features were cut to meet the deadline.

The core changes (labeled buttons and the new rows) shipped. The alert didn’t, so people who hadn’t heard about the opening might get confused. We covered the gap with emails, a landing page, FAQs and tutorials.

Other problems at launch:
notes: My biggest regret: the alert didn’t ship
list: The first deploy failed, pushing the launch back a day
Many users didn’t know the difference between a subdomain and a top-level domain

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Working for the government is hard, but it can be deeply rewarding. Despite all the issues:
list: 35,000 new .ar domains registered in the first two months
Large customers praised how simple the process was

sections.heading: Extra: renewing multiple domains
sections.text: Renewing several domains at once sounds simple. It wasn’t.
sections.caption: Select several domains and renew them in one step.
sections.alt: Domain list with checkboxes and a Renew domains button

detail.summary: How small, targeted UX changes helped open Argentina’s .ar domain to the public, with 35,000 domains registered in the first two months.

sections.heading: Case study: Sello de Tiempo (Timestamp)
sections.text:
An institution in the BFA community built a timestamp tool: a way to prove that a digital document existed at a given moment and hasn’t changed since. They built it first, and then asked me to “put the design on it.”

So I started from a very basic app and worked out how to make it usable and appealing. There were no front-end developers on the project, so I built the front end myself, in Vue.js, a framework I had never used before.
notes: They had built it first. My job was to make it usable.

sections.text: The flow was simple: pick a file, stamp it, then verify that it was added to the blockchain. This is what they sent me:
sections.caption: The original app: drop a file, stamp it, wait, done.
sections.alt: The original timestamp app: four basic screens with dashed boxes and plain buttons

sections.heading: A brand-new timestamp
sections.text: I started from the BFA website’s styles, which were based on Bootstrap, so the tool would feel like part of the platform.
sections.caption: The first screen looks different but works the same.
sections.alt: Sello de Tiempo 2.0: upload screen to drag or select files

sections.caption: Users can now add several files and stamp or verify them all at once.
sections.alt: Sello de Tiempo 2.0: a file ready to verify or stamp, with its hash

sections.caption: Success: a read-only verification link the user can copy and share.
sections.alt: Sello de Tiempo 2.0: file sent successfully, with a verification link

sections.caption: Verified: the block number and date prove the file hasn’t changed since.
sections.alt: Sello de Tiempo 2.0: verification result with block number and date

sections.heading: Outcome
sections.text: The app was a success and was presented at blockchain events. Other teams have kept improving it since.
notes: The whole project lives in BFA’s private GitLab repository

detail.summary: Turning Argentina’s public blockchain from an idea into a brand, a website, web apps and a conference.

projects.title: Viñetas Sueltas
projects.content: Ten years of websites for an international comics festival, each one built from scratch in two weeks.

detail.client: Viñetas Sueltas is a nonprofit that runs an international comics festival in Buenos Aires. I co-founded it, and I designed and built its website from 2008 to 2017.
detail.context: Web development changed a lot between 2008 and 2017, but one constraint never did: two weeks to build the site from scratch, on top of my day job.

sections.text:
With a solid setup from 2016 already in place, this year was all about the design.

The poster was drawn by an American artist, and I followed it from the first rough sketches to the final art. The sketches shaped the festival’s visual language, and the final poster gave me the color palette.
sections.alt: Viñetas Sueltas festival website, 2017

sections.text:
This year I rebuilt everything from scratch with a proper build system, using every tool I could find to make the two-week sprint easier.

The guest list lived in a JSON file, so adding, removing or editing guests took seconds. I set up Gulp, Bower and Bootstrap, and off I went.

I talked with the illustrator early about the poster’s colors and composition, and I knew the guest list would arrive at the last minute. Knowing where the poster was headed made every section easier to design.
sections.alt: Viñetas Sueltas festival website, 2016

sections.text: A site that’s online two weeks a year is perfect as a single page. It was also my first dive into media queries and responsive design, and a lot of fun.
sections.alt: Viñetas Sueltas festival website, 2012

sections.text:
Steve Jobs had declared war on Flash, and we were going crazy. HTML came back strong, and I had to return to markup, which I’d left behind in the days of tables and spacer GIFs.

The result was cleaner and more readable. Not responsive, though: in 2010, I didn’t even own a smartphone.
sections.alt: Viñetas Sueltas festival website, 2010

sections.text: I reused the 2008 site and brought the mascot to life with character animation. Apparently I was deep into grunge back then, and I went way over the top.
sections.alt: Viñetas Sueltas festival website, 2009

sections.text:
A friend called: the independent comics festival we were starting needed a website, and it needed it within a week.

It may look rough today, but back then, pulling a blog’s RSS feed into a Flash site was a big deal.
sections.alt: Viñetas Sueltas festival website, 2008

detail.summary: Ten years, six websites, one constraint: two weeks to build each one from scratch, on top of my day job.
